You are an Opus research worker on the Fortress revival (repo: your worktree of /home/user/fortress). Read these first, in order — they are your complete context and binding rules:

1. /home/user/fortress/CLAUDE.md (build env: JDK 25 exports, unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD i.e. your worktree root, ant compileAll ~90s, FORTRESS_THREADS=1 for all runs, component name must equal filename)
2. explorations/microgpt-iteration2-plan.md — sections "Standing design rules", "Verified facts", "Worker discipline" apply verbatim to you (spec-first authority; never end at first interpreter error; no single-data-point rules; worktree only, no commits, no tracked-file modifications)
3. explorations/expressiveness-review.md — known verified facts, don't re-derive
4. explorations/repo-internals.md — architecture map if you need to trace interpreter code

RESEARCH QUESTIONS (from Pavol):

**Q1 — Type aliases.** Does Fortress support naming a type as an alias of another (e.g. `KVCache` as an alias for `List[\List[\Value\]\]` or similar)? Search the Specification/ LaTeX sources (NOT any PDF) for type alias / `type` declarations / `dim`-like abbreviation mechanisms for ordinary types. Then probe the interpreter: does whatever the spec sanctions parse and run? If true aliases don't exist or don't work, characterize the nearest working substitutes (empty trait extension? wrapper object? just a comment?) with probes, and classify each failure: implementation gap vs design limit (vs "spec never had it").

**Q2 — Dimensions and units.** The spec famously has physical units (meters, m/s, dimension checking, `dim`/`unit` declarations, SI units library). Find the spec chapter(s) and summarize what the language promises. Then determine what the 2012 interpreter actually implements: search the interpreter source and Library/ (is there a units library file? DimUnit handling in the evaluator/type checker?), and write small probes — declare a dim/unit, multiply meters by seconds, dimension-check an error case. Report exactly what parses, what evaluates, what checks, with errors verbatim. Prior art hint: check whether any tests under ProjectFortress/tests or the static tests exercise dimensions — that's evidence of implemented surface.

**Q3 — Pedagogical application to microgpt2.** Read explorations/microgpt2.fss (the flagship). Given your Q1/Q2 findings, assess honestly: where would naming types (Token, TokenId, Logits, KVCache, ProbDist, Embedding...) or units-style typing add pedagogical value to the microgpt notation, and where would it be noise? The mission (in the plan file) is literature-correspondence judged by eye — ML papers don't write units, but they DO write named spaces (t ∈ V, x ∈ ℝᵈ). Would type aliases let the Fortress signatures echo the paper's "∈" statements? Sketch (and probe-run, if aliases work) 2-3 concrete before/after signature examples from microgpt2.fss. Give a recommendation with reasons: adopt / adopt narrowly / don't adopt. Do NOT modify microgpt2.fss itself.

DELIVERABLES to /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/bdff267d-67dc-5bb9-b970-8c3dfaa634b6/scratchpad/aliases-units/:
- report.md — findings organized by Q1/Q2/Q3, every claim backed by spec citation (file:line) or a probe file, errors verbatim, failures classified
- probes as p*_name.fss files (runnable; note which ones you actually ran and their output)
Report every dead end with the error verbatim and the spec section consulted. Be thorough — your budget is generous; the coordinator's is not, so make report.md self-contained.

1	# Fortress revival
2	
3	This is @palimondo's revival of Sun/Oracle's **Fortress** programming language
4	(Guy Steele's HPC language, 2003–2012; interpreter + partial JVM compiler,
5	BSD-licensed). The repo carries the full available git history (5397 commits,
6	root 2007-01-04, HEAD Aug 2012) with pluckyporcupine's Scala 2.10.7/Java 9
7	migration grafted on top as a tree overlay — see the commit messages of the
8	graft commits for lineage and attribution. Working mode: Claude explains the
9	codebase and produces documentation and experiments as we go; Pavol decides
10	what gets committed. The full collaboration protocol — roles, tone, how work
11	is presented, commit discipline, delegation — is in
12	`explorations/protocol.md`; read it at session start.
13	
14	## Build and run (verified: Ubuntu 24.04 container, JDK 25 — current rung)
15	
16	```bash
17	apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant  # JDK 8/11/17/21 also still work (all gated green)
18	export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
19	export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH
20	export FORTRESS_HOME=<repo root>
21	unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS                          # proxy trust-store options confuse ant's JVM forks
22	cd $FORTRESS_HOME && ant compileAll              # ~80 s
23	./bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss      # interpreter ("walk") — this works
24	```
25	
26	Toolchain (2026-08-21): Scala 2.13.18 (build.xml drives scalac via
27	`scala.tools.nsc.Main` directly — Scala 2.13 dropped the `scala.tools.ant`
28	tasks), ASM 9.10.1 (vendored in
29	`ProjectFortress/third_party/asm/`; watch out — Fortress's own
30	`asmbytecodeoptimizer.Opcodes` shadows `org.objectweb.asm.Opcodes` in that
31	package), `-source/-target 1.8` and emitted classfiles V1_6 (both now
32	merely conventions — ASM 9 unblocks raising them as a deliberate later
33	step), sources compiled as UTF-8 (all sources were already valid UTF-8;
34	the old ISO-8859-1 javac attributes just mis-decoded comments),
35	work-stealing runtime on stdlib `java.util.concurrent` ForkJoin (vendored
36	jsr166y retired); see `explorations/modernization-plan.md` for the ladder
37	and current rung.
38	
39	Facts that save time:
40	
41	- **Both execution paths work.** `fortress <file>.fss` interprets directly.
42	  The bytecode compiler path (`fortress compile` + `fortress run`) also works
43	  on JDK 8 — pluckyporcupine's "compiled programs don't run" is wrong here —
44	  but has two traps: imported library components (`System`,
45	  `CompilerSystem`) must be explicitly `fortress compile`d into the cache
46	  first, and **stale caches** cause a misleading
47	  `NoSuchMethodError: fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println(...)` — wipe
48	  `default_repository/caches/*` and recompile in library order (recipe in
49	  `explorations/repo-internals.md`). The compiler is incomplete (some
50	  constructs still `sayWhat`), not broken. See
51	  `explorations/test-baseline-jdk8.md`.
52	- **`ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only via the compiler path** — its July
53	  2012 upgrade imports `System.getProperty`/`CompilerSystem.args`, which the
54	  interpreter can't resolve. Use `explorations/*.fss` as interpreter smoke
55	  tests.
56	- **Test suite (2026-08-19): fully green.** `ant testFast` (~1,400 tests
57	  incl. the full compiler suite) and `ant testSystem` (382 interpreter
58	  tests) both pass with zero failures — the first fully green suite in this
59	  lineage (the 2012 mainline ended with 7 red). History and the two fixes:
60	  `explorations/test-baseline-jdk8.md`.
61	- The interpreter requires filename (sans `.fss`) == component name.
62	- If scalac fails with arity errors in `S*Pattern` nodes, the generated AST
63	  sources are stale relative to `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`:
64	  `touch ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast && ant compileAll` regenerates.
65	- Interpreter caches live in `default_repository/caches/` (gitignored); wipe
66	  them if library edits seem to have no effect.
67	- Architecture map, name-resolution rules, cache anatomy, test-harness
68	  mechanics, and git-archaeology techniques: `explorations/repo-internals.md`
69	  — read it before diving into the source.
70	
71	## Layout
72	
73	- Original Fortress tree: everything not listed below — do not modify
74	  casually; it is the historical artifact being revived.
75	- `explorations/` — revival-era experiments and writeups (ours; verified
76	  running programs).
77	- `research/` — the Guy Steele corpus: `research/README.md` is a committed
78	  links-only index; `research/extracts/` holds committed working notes;
79	  `research/decks/` is **gitignored** (copyrighted PDFs, dropped in per
80	  session, never committed).
81	- `Specification/` + `Specification-1.0-frozen/` — the language spec LaTeX
82	  (in-repo, richer than the published PDF; building it is untested).
83	
84	## Project goals (rough order)
85	
86	1. ~~Baseline the 2012 test suite~~ DONE — fully green on JDK 8 (see above).
87	2. Modernization ladder — **approved plan, standing orders, and current rung:
88	   `explorations/modernization-plan.md`** (Scala 2.12 ✓ → JDK 11 → UTF-8 →
89	   jsr166y→j.u.c. → JDK 17/21 → ASM 9 → Scala 2.13 eval; each rung gated on
90	   the fully green suite; CI early).
91	3. Complex numbers: the spec promises ℂ but zero complex arithmetic shipped;
92	   seed is `explorations/complex_ring.fss`.
93	4. Fix the bytecode compiler path — characterized 2026-08-24: the gap is
94	   the compiler's tiny prelude library, not codegen; prioritized worklist
95	   and measured 6.8–8.9× payoff in `explorations/compiled-path-gaps.md`.
96	5. Grow the Steele research corpus (`research/README.md` lists open hunts).
97	6. microgpt.fss — port Karpathy's 243-line dependency-free GPT (scalar
98	   autodiff, char-level transformer) to interpreter Fortress as an
99	   executable-paper showcase; feasibility map and staging:
100	   `explorations/microgpt-port.md`.
101	
102	Claims in old READMEs (root `README.txt`, pluckyporcupine's `README.md`,
103	`NOTES.md`) describe *their* eras, not the current tree — verify against the
104	code before acting on them.

1	# microgpt iteration 2: plan for the from-scratch notation exploration
2	
3	Approved by Pavol 2026-08-26. This file is the complete context for every
4	worker in the run. Read it fully before doing anything.
5	
6	## Mission (approved verbatim in essence)
7	
8	Test Fortress's founding claim on the best possible specimen. The claim:
9	the gap between how ML literature states a transformer's mathematics and
10	how programs implement it is a language defect that Fortress was built
11	to close. The specimen: Karpathy's microgpt, the smallest complete GPT.
12	The test: construct, in running and verified Fortress, the notation that
13	lets each building block of the model be stated so that its typeset form
14	and the literature's own formula sit side by side and the reader can
15	judge the distance **by eye**. The deliverable teaches two things at
16	once and inseparably: how a GPT works (a reader starting from zero
17	leaves understanding it) and how the notation is constructed (what the
18	language gives, what it must be taught, and what it cannot yet say).
19	Where the correspondence fails, the failure is shown and classified —
20	implementation gap (revival worklist) versus design limit. Everything
21	shown runs; correctness is anchored to the Python reference; the
22	process is documented.
23	
24	**Not the mission** (named local minima — do not fall into them):
25	fidelity to Steele's 2015 slide idioms; preservation of any prior
26	rung's code structure (this iteration starts FROM SCRATCH); the golden
27	check as an aesthetic constraint (it is a correctness instrument only);
28	interpreter speed (measured, reported, never steering notation).
29	
30	## Standing design rules (from Pavol, binding)
31	
32	1. **No custom BIG operators** (`BIG OPLUS`, `BIG BOXPLUS`, any new
33	   glyph) unless the form is (a) genuinely the prevalent way ML
34	   literature writes that mathematics, or (b) provably the only working
35	   way in current Fortress, with the spec-vs-implementation gap
36	   documented. The ML literature writes Σ, Π, 𝔼, max — never custom big
37	   operators. Glyph imitation of Σ is not Σ. Default: named functions
38	   (`sum(...)`) over comprehensions; the genuine library `SUM` where
39	   summands are `Number`s (e.g. over `.data` inside a sum-node
40	   constructor).
41	2. **The specification is the first authority** for any language
42	   question: `Specification/` LaTeX sources (byte-identical to
43	   1.0-frozen in all chapters audited so far). Order of authority:
44	   spec → `explorations/expressiveness-review.md` (audited findings
45	   with probes) → library sources → fresh empirical probe. Never end a
46	   design path at the first interpreter error: check what the spec
47	   sanctions (the vector×matrix "impossibility" had a documented
48	   escape, the Meet Rule / `excludes`), then record divergence.
49	3. **No single-data-point rules.** Any claimed constraint ("always
50	   parenthesize X", "Y is impossible") requires either a spec citation
51	   or two independent probes, recorded.
52	
53	## Verified facts (do not re-derive; probes in `explorations/spec-probes/`)
54	
55	- List/comprehension element-type ascriptions `[\T\]` are needed ONLY
56	  when elements' runtime class differs from the target (numeric
57	  literals → `FloatLiteral`; nested `ArrayList[\…\]` under invariant
58	  `List`). For concrete object element types (like an autodiff node)
59	  they are redundant. Return types on definitions are optional
60	  (inference chapter in the spec is a stub; the implementation infers).
61	  The `zip` static argument is mandatory.
62	- The algebraic tower that exists: `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` and
63	  `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]` only (`FortressLibrary.fss:328,340`).
64	  Extending `MultiplicativeRing[\V\]` with `one`/`TIMES` inherits
65	  juxtaposition, binary minus, `zero` (precedent:
66	  `explorations/complex_ring.fss`). The spec's full
67	  `Monoid…Field` chapter ships only as commented-out
68	  `Library/incomplete/…INCOMPLETE`.
69	- Two juxtaposition (or any operator) overloads on `(List,List)` shapes
70	  are illegal — but **mutually excluding carrier traits make both
71	  directions legal** (library's own Vector/Matrix at
72	  `FortressLibrary.fss:2634,2641` via `Rank1 excludes Rank2`; probes
73	  `p7_excludes.fss`, `p14_genwrap.fss` — a six-line carrier object also
74	  buys `|x|`, `x[i]`, `x[r]`, generator integration, `.map`, clean
75	  renders).
76	- `SUM` is closed to user types three ways (library `Number` seal,
77	  spec's no-static-param-overloading rule, desugarer's one-nullary-
78	  registration-per-name). Coercion parses but is unwired. Multifix
79	  dispatch is unimplemented. `Number` already has `SQRT`.
80	- Real parse traps (verified): chained subscripts need `(m[i])[j]`
81	  (grammatical by design, `concrete-syntax.tex:921`); `^` after a call
82	  or dotted field needs parens; `|w||>` and `/|` need a space; `V`
83	  cannot name a variable while object `V` is in scope. FALSIFIED trap,
84	  do not propagate: "comprehension bodies ending in a subscript need
85	  parens" — they don't.
86	- Interpreter performance law: run everything `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`
87	  (idle-worker micro-forking makes 2 workers slower than 1).
88	- `nat`-parameterized user vectors with dimension-checked ops run
89	  (`p9_natvec.fss`) — available as a design ingredient, not a mandate.
90	
91	## Correctness anchors
92	
93	- The golden check: deterministic-weight config in
94	  `explorations/microgpt.fss` `goldenCheck()` — 15 logits + mean loss
95	  1.228662661701597 + 5 gradients at 1e-9. Any complete candidate must
96	  pass it (values are architecture-level truths, independent of
97	  notation). Nucleus-stage candidates use the lighter analytic checks
98	  (style of `explorations/mgnative_a.fss` run()) or hand-computed
99	  attention values.
100	- Reference implementations for BEHAVIOR only (not style):
101	  `explorations/microgpt.fss` (v1), `microgpt_native.fss`,
102	  `microgpt_paper.fss`. Architecture facts: 1 layer, heads structural,
103	  rmsnorm without gain, no biases, plain relu, causal by history,
104	  Adam β₁ .85 β₂ .99 lr .01 linear decay, BOS=26 vocab 27.
105	
106	## Fitness function
107	
108	For each building block, typeset the Fortress definition with Fortify
109	(recipe in any `explorations/fortify/*.tic` header: fortick → latex →
110	dvisvgm; rasterize with chromium `--headless --no-sandbox --screenshot`)
111	and hold it against the literature's formula for that block:
112	
113	- h⁰ = Wₑ[t] + Wₚ[i]
114	- RMSNorm(x) = x / √(x·x/d + ε)
115	- A(q,kⱼ) = q·kⱼ/√d_k ; weights = softmax over j≤i ; out = Σⱼ pⱼvⱼ
116	  (vector form: softmax(qKᵀ/√d_k)V)
117	- FFN(x) = W₂ relu(W₁ x)
118	- L = −log softmax(logits)_y
119	- Adam: element-wise update equations (index form IS the literature here)
120	
121	Judged by eye: would a reader of the paper recognize the line? Every
122	departure needs a reason from the classification {implementation gap,
123	design limit, deliberate-with-reason}.
124	
125	## Deliverables ladder (this workflow: nucleus stage)
126	
127	Each design candidate delivers a NUCLEUS, not the full model: the
128	notation layer it proposes plus running, checked implementations of
129	rmsnorm, softmax, one-head attention (score+weights+blend over a
130	history), and ffn, over the candidate's own autodiff value type (a
131	minimal tape engine is fine; reuse of engine A's *concepts* is allowed,
132	code written fresh). Plus: its Fortify render sheet, a rasterized PNG,
133	and a design memo (what the language gave / had to be taught / can't
134	say; every deviation classified; what the full model would look like —
135	sketch the forward pass in the candidate's notation).
136	
137	Full-model implementation, presentation build, and integration happen
138	AFTER Pavol-side judgment of the candidates — not in this workflow.
139	
140	## Presentation (context for memos; built after judgment)
141	
142	The rebuilt page interleaves tightly: short concept prose per block,
143	then immediately the paired lines — the literature's formula and the
144	Fortress definition's render, adjacent, no repetition of the formula in
145	prose, no tan "the paper writes" echo boxes, never a big code block
146	followed by explanation. New content queued: the honest-loss-curve
147	section (explorations/training-dynamics.md + chart) and the
148	PRNG/SplitMix lineage note (Fortress's parallelism → Steele's 2014
149	splittable PRNGs; explorations/prng-findings.md). The three prior rungs
150	(transliteration → index → carriers) remain the notation-ladder
151	exhibit.
152	
153	## Worker discipline
154	
155	Worktree only; `ant compileAll` once (env per CLAUDE.md: JDK 25
156	exports, unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD); no commits, no
157	pushes, no tracked-file modifications; deliverables copied to the
158	session scratchpad under your candidate's name; timings indicative
159	(shared box). Report every dead end with the error verbatim and the
160	spec section consulted.
161	
162	## Judgment (2026-08-26, coordinating session; full brief: candidates-decision-brief.md in session scratchpad, mirrored below in spirit)
163	
164	The model notation is the **carriers ⊕ tower merge**; spartan survives as
165	the page's measurement exhibit (its verified price list of what each line
166	of machinery buys). Decisions on the brief's open questions:
167	
168	1. Axis weighting: fidelity and machinery-as-content together — the merge
169	   with tower's inheritance-ledger narrative serves both mission halves.
170	2. Weights typeset **bold** (`_W1` → 𝐖₁): bold-matrix is a genuine,
171	   prevalent ML register; italic-capital subscripts are unreachable
172	   (spec numeral rule + Fortify roman rule — classified design/toolchain
173	   limit, stated on the page).
174	3. **Adopt `^T`**: the flagship attention line becomes the literature's
175	   own `softmax(q Kᵀ/√d_k) V`; the one-line transpose operator is itself
176	   a teachable exhibit.
177	4. **Keep the visible max-shift**, in tower's form: `StandardMax[\V\]`
178	   opens the genuine library `BIG MAX` (no `.data` leak) — an honest
179	   numerics point Karpathy also keeps, and the counterpoint to sealed Σ.
180	5. **Bind `d = |x|` / use `d_k` fields** so the paper's symbols survive
181	   and `|·|` is never misread as a norm.
182	6. Spartan's price list and falsified-trap hygiene become page content.
183	7. Per-head plumbing stays as comprehensions — the literature's
184	   `head₁…head_h` ellipsis made precise, not hidden behind machinery.
185	8. Render sheets show the machinery (carriers, lifts, extends-clauses
186	   framed as the inheritance ledger; `sum()`'s body framed as the
187	   autodiff-sees-Σ lesson) — the mission's second half is not curated
188	   away.
189	9. Mandated cleanups: define carrier `=` (the reflexive-false landmine);
190	   apply all judge reclassifications (carriers D2/D5, tower's `Vv` and
191	   "library fiat"); engine node named `Value` freeing the letter `V`;
192	   the loose-vs-tight-slash footnote; every full-model claim gated on
193	   the golden check.
194	
195	Build target: `explorations/microgpt2.fss`, plus per-block render
196	figures (one small .tic/.svg per block) for the interleaved page.

content.content:
1	<!-- Produced by a delegated spec-audit worker session during the microgpt-native
2	     exploration; commissioned by Pavol's review of 2026-08-26. Probe programs:
3	     explorations/spec-probes/. Design journal: explorations/microgpt-native.md. -->
4	
5	# Adversarial expressiveness audit: `explorations/microgpt_paper.fss` vs. the Fortress specification
6	
7	Audit date 2026-08-26. Spec read from the LaTeX sources in `Specification/` (working draft).
8	Every one of the ten chapters cited below is **byte-identical** in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`
9	(verified by `diff`), so nothing here turns on which spec you read.
10	
11	Interpreter: `./bin/fortress` on JDK 25, per `CLAUDE.md`. All probes are in
12	`probes-spec/` next to this file. Tracked files were never modified: the
13	golden-gated trials ran on `explorations/mgprobe.fss`, a scratch copy whose
14	`run()` is `goldenCheck()` only; it was removed after each run and
15	`git status --porcelain` is empty.
16	
17	Classification: **(a) WORKS today** — spec feature, interpreter supports it, we
18	failed to use it. **(b) SPEC-ONLY** — spec promises it, implementation does not
19	deliver. **(c) DELIBERATE** — our way is defensible, reason stated.
20	
21	Counts: **6 (a) WORKS · 8 (b) SPEC-ONLY · 6 (c) DELIBERATE**, plus 3 places
22	where the spec is silent and the library is the only authority.
23	
24	- (a) findings 1, 3, 4, 10, 11, 15
25	- (b) findings 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 12, 13, 14
26	- (c) verdicts in findings 5, 6, 7, 10, and the four listed in 16
27	
28	---
29	
30	## Verified simplification bundle (all (a); golden check PASSes)
31	
32	Applied together to a scratch copy of the file and run: **`golden transformer
33	forward/backward vs Python reference: PASS`** (probe files
34	`probes-spec/mgprobe_s3.fss`, `mgprobe_s4.fss`, `mgprobe_s5.fss`;
35	baseline `mgprobe_base.fss`).
36	
37	| # | Change | Lines touched |
38	|---|--------|---------------|
39	| A1 | drop `[\V\]` from every list aggregate/comprehension whose elements are `V` | 26 |
40	| A2 | `object V ... extends AdditiveGroup[\V\]`, delete hand-written binary `-` | +1 / −1 |
41	| A3 | delete `opr SQRT(n: ZZ32): RR64` — the library already has it | −1 |
42	| A4 | drop the return-type annotation from the 11 notation-layer declarations | 11 |
43	| A5 | (optional, also PASSes) full `MultiplicativeRing[\V\]`: define `TIMES`, inherit `juxtaposition` | +2 / −1 |
44	
45	---
46	
47	# Findings, ordered by impact on the program's notation
48	
49	---
50	
51	## 1. (a) WORKS — the `[\V\]` on every aggregate is redundant: 26 of them
52	
53	**Spec.** `Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex`, §`list-expr`:
54	
55	> The type of a list expression is `List[\T\]` where `T` is the union type of
56	> the types of all element expressions.
57	
58	The element type is *inferred*. Static args on an aggregate are optional in the
59	grammar (`LeftEncloser option{StaticArgs} …`, §`aggregate-expr`; same in
60	`Specification/basic/expressions/comprehensions.tex`).
61	
62	**Current code.** Ascribed everywhere, e.g. line 58:
63	
64	```
65	  opr +(self, o: V): V = V(data + o.data, <|[\V\] self, o|>, <|[\RR64\] 1.0, 1.0|>)
66	```
67	
68	and line 157:
69	
70	```
71	  <|[\V\] (w[r] DOT x) | r <- 0#|w| |>
72	```
73	
74	**Probe.** `probes-spec/p1_infer.fss` — unascribed literals and comprehensions of
75	a user object type infer correctly. Golden-gated across the whole program in
76	`mgprobe_s5.fss`: **all 26** `<|[\V\] …|>` occurrences drop, golden check PASSes.
77	
78	**Simplification.**
79	
80	```
81	- opr +(self, o: V): V = V(data + o.data, <|[\V\] self, o|>, <|[\RR64\] 1.0, 1.0|>)
82	+ opr +(self, o: V): V = V(data + o.data, <| self, o |>, <|[\RR64\] 1.0, 1.0|>)
83	
84	-   <|[\V\] (w[r] DOT x) | r <- 0#|w| |>
85	+   <| (w[r] DOT x) | r <- 0#|w| |>
86	```
87	
88	**But — the `[\RR64\]` and `[\List[…]\]` ascriptions are NOT redundant, and the
89	reason is finding 2.** `probes-spec/p2_ascribe.fss`:
90	
91	```
92	Unification error: Closure/Constructor for V param 3 ($grads:List[\RR64\])
93	got arg ArrayList[\FloatLiteral\] of type ArrayList[\FloatLiteral\]
94	```
95	
96	and, once the `[\RR64\]` on `<| o.data, data |>` is dropped, `ArrayList[\Float\]`.
97	Dropping `[\List[\V\]\]` gives `ArrayList[\ArrayList[\V\]\]`. So the interpreter
98	computes the aggregate's element type from the **runtime class** of the elements
99	(`FloatLiteral`, `Float`, `ArrayList[\V\]`), not from their declared type, and
100	`List` is invariant. That is only harmless when the elements' runtime class *is*
101	the target element type — true for `V` (a concrete object), false for `RR64` and
102	for `List[\…\]`. The authors generalised from the `RR64` case (which really does
103	need the ascription) to the `V` case (which does not).
104	
105	---
106	
107	## 2. (b) SPEC-ONLY — declaration-site covariance: the root cause of all remaining ascriptions
108	
109	**Spec.** `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex` (~line 339):
110	
111	> Trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of themselves.
112	> For example, we can write `trait C[\S\] extends C[\T\] where {S extends T, T
113	> extends Object} end`. … Effectively, we have expressed the fact that the
114	> static parameter `S` of `C` is covariant.
115	
116	If `List` were declared this way, `List[\Float\] <: List[\RR64\]` and
117	`List[\ArrayList[\V\]\] <: List[\List[\V\]\]`, and **every** remaining ascription
118	in the file (and `x.zip[\V\](y)`, finding 9) would go away.
119	
120	**Library.** `Library/List.fss:112` — `trait List[\E\] extends { AnyList,
121	LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] }`, invariant. And `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2243`
122	carries the comment `(* TODO: fix when Number is covariant. *)`.
123	
124	**Probe.** `probes-spec/p16_covar.fss` writes the spec's idiom verbatim:
125	
126	```
127	trait Co[\S\] extends Co[\T\] where { S extends T, T extends Object }
128	```
129	```
130	p16_covar.fss:6:27: T is undefined.
131	p16_covar.fss:6:49: T is undefined.
132	```
133	
134	The interpreter does not bind where-clause type variables in an `extends` clause.
135	Corroborating evidence that the library authors hit the same wall:
136	`Library/CovariantCollection.fss` is an entire hand-rolled covariant list built
137	out of `typecase` and explicit `upward[\R, I extends R, T extends R\]` lifting
138	functions — the workaround for the feature the spec describes in one line.
139	
140	**Revival-worklist item, high value:** this single gap is responsible for most of
141	the notational noise in `microgpt_paper.fss`, in `microgpt_native.fss`, and in
142	`Library/CovariantCollection.fss` itself.
143	
144	---
145	
146	## 3. (a) WORKS — `V` should join the numeric tower, exactly as `C` does
147	
148	**Spec.** `Specification/advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex`,
149	§`monoids-groups-rings-fields`, defines `Monoid`, `CommutativeMonoid`, `Group`,
150	`AbelianGroup`, `SemiRing`, `Ring`, `CommutativeRing`, `Field` — each as a trait
151	carrying default methods derived from the abstract ones.
152	
153	**Library (the only authority in practice).** `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`
154	implements *two* of them: `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` (line 328) and
155	`MultiplicativeRing[\T\]` (line 340). `AdditiveGroup` gives, free:
156	
157	```
158	    getter zero(): T = self - self
159	    opr -(self, other: T): T = self + (-other)
160	    opr -(self) : T = self.zero - self
161	```
162	
163	**Current code.** `V` extends nothing, and line 63 hand-writes precisely the
164	`AdditiveGroup` default:
165	
166	```
167	  opr -(self, o: V): V = self + (-o)
168	```
169	
170	The in-house precedent `explorations/complex_ring.fss` does the opposite:
171	`object C … extends MultiplicativeRing[\C\]` inherits juxtaposition, binary
172	minus and `zero` from three chained defaults.
173	
174	**Probes.** `probes-spec/p4_addgroup.fss` (AdditiveGroup) and
175	`probes-spec/p5_ring.fss` (MultiplicativeRing) both run; golden-gated in
176	`mgprobe_s3.fss` / `mgprobe_s4.fss`.
177	
178	**Simplification (minimum-cost form, A2).**
179	
180	```
181	  object V(var data: RR64, children: List[\V\], grads: List[\RR64\])
182	+         extends AdditiveGroup[\V\]
183	    …
184	-   opr -(self, o: V): V = self + (-o)
185	```
186	
187	The `opr +(self, c: RR64)` overload keeps resolving alongside the inherited
188	generic `+` (verified). The full-ring form (A5) additionally inherits
189	`juxtaposition` from `TIMES` at the cost of `getter one()` and
190	`opr ^(self, n: AnyIntegral)`; both `^` overloads (`AnyIntegral` and `RR64`)
191	coexist because `AnyIntegral <: RR64` makes the pair a legal Subtype-Rule
192	overloading. Recommend A2 as the change and A5 as the statement of intent —
193	the reason `C` is a `MultiplicativeRing` is that it *is* one, and so is `V`.
194	
195	---
196	
197	## 4. (a) WORKS — the vector×matrix overload the header calls impossible **is** buildable
198	
199	This is the file's own boxed exception (header lines 30–49):
200	
201	> ONE spec item could not be built as written. … The interpreter rejects the
202	> pair: *first parameters `p:[List[\V\],List[\List[\V\]\]]` and
203	> `w:[List[\List[\V\]\],List[\V\]]` are unrelated (neither subtype, excludes,
204	> nor equal) and no excluding pair is present* — two instantiations of the SAME
205	> generic trait are not seen as disjoint.
206	
207	**The library does exactly this, and it works.** `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`
208	declares **both** directions:
209	
210	```
211	opr juxtaposition[\ T extends Number, nat n, nat m \]
212	     (me:Matrix[\T,n,m\], v:Vector[\T,m\]):Vector[\T,n\] = me.rmul(v)      (:2634)
213	
214	opr juxtaposition[\ T extends Number, nat n, nat m \]
215	     (v:Vector[\T,n\], me:Matrix[\T,n,m\]):Vector[\T,m\] = me.lmul(v)      (:2641)
216	```
217	
218	It is legal because the two carriers are **mutually excluding traits**, not two
219	instantiations of one:
220	
221	```
222	trait Rank1 extends { Rank[\1\]} excludes { Rank2, Rank3, Number, String }   (:1599)
223	trait Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\] extends { AnyVector, Array1[…] }    (:2189)
224	trait Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\] extends { AnyMatrix, Array2[…] } (:2497)
225	```
226	
227	The blocker was never "two instantiations of a generic trait"; it was
228	"`List[\V\]` and `List[\List[\V\]\]` do not *exclude*". The spec agrees the
229	instantiations are not disjoint — `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex`
230	explicitly permits `trait C[\S\] extends C[\T\]`, so `A[\ZZ32\]` and
231	`A[\Boolean\]` really can share a subtype, and the hopeful comment in
232	`ProjectFortress/tests/doubledOverloading3.fss` ("we should consider these
233	instantiations to be disjoint (right right?)") is wrong *per spec*. The remedy
234	the spec offers is §`more-specific-rule` (the Meet Rule): "either `P excludes Q`
235	or there is a declaration `f(P ∩ Q)` in the scope". The library takes the
236	`excludes` branch.
237	
238	**Probe 1** — the exclusion alone (`probes-spec/p7_excludes.fss`):
239	
240	```
241	trait Rank1V excludes Rank2V end
242	trait Rank2V excludes Rank1V end
243	object Vec(xs: List[\V\]) extends Rank1V …
244	object Mat(rows: List[\Vec\]) extends Rank2V …
245	opr juxtaposition(m: Mat, x: Vec): Vec = …
246	opr juxtaposition(p: Vec, m: Mat): Vec = …
247	```
248	```
249	m x = Vec<|V(1.0), V(6.0)|>
250	x m = Vec<|V(1.0), V(6.0)|>
251	```
252	
253	**Probe 2** — the objection the header raises against wrappers ("no wrapper
254	objects, so the renders carry no field noise") is answerable. Make the carriers
255	library generators (`probes-spec/p14_genwrap.fss`):
256	
257	```
258	object Vec(xs: List[\V\]) extends { Rank1V, ZeroIndexed[\V\], DelegatedIndexed[\V,ZZ32\] }
259	  getter asString(): String = "" xs
260	  getter indices(): Generator[\ZZ32\] = 0#|xs|
261	  opr |self| : ZZ32 = |xs|
262	  opr [i: ZZ32]: V = xs[i]
263	  opr [r: Range[\ZZ32\]]: ZeroIndexed[\V\] = Vec(xs[r])
264	end
265	```
266	```
267	m x  = <|V(1.0), V(6.0)|>
268	x m  = <|V(1.0), V(6.0)|>
269	|x|  = 2   x[1] = V(2.0)
270	comprehension over Vec: <|1.0, 2.0|>
271	for over Mat:
272	  row <|V(1.0), V(0.0)|>
273	  row <|V(0.0), V(3.0)|>
274	```
275	
276	Six lines of carrier per rank buys `|x|`, `x[i]`, `x[r]`, `u <- x`, `seq(x)`,
277	`.map`, `.reduce`, no field noise in renders — **and both juxtaposition
278	directions**, which is the attention blend written the way the brief asked:
279	
280	```
281	- BIG BOXPLUS[j <- 0#|p|] p[j] Vv[j]
282	+ p Vv
283	```
284	
285	**Cost, stated honestly.** This is a structural rewrite of the notation layer
286	(every `List[\V\]` becomes `Vec`, every `List[\List[\V\]\]` becomes `Mat`,
287	`BIG BOXPLUS` and `VecConcat` and `vecsum` disappear, the three-different-names
288	workaround for `Vec.Vec`/`Mat.Vec`/`Vec.Mat` disappears). It is not a
289	line-for-line edit. But the header's claim that it *cannot be done* is false,
290	and the header's stated reason (generic instantiations are not disjoint) is the
291	right diagnosis of the wrong problem.
292	
293	---
294	
295	## 5. (b) SPEC-ONLY — coercion: `konst(…)` and the RR64 overload triplication are unavoidable *today*
296	
297	**Spec.** `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex` — a 906-line chapter.
298	§`coercion-declarations`: "To declare that trait `U` allows a coercion from type
299	`T`, the declaration of trait `U` must provide a coercion declaration whose
300	parameter type is `T`." §`coercion` lists the contexts, including "arguments to
301	functionals and constructors where the corresponding parameters have declared
302	types". `Specification/basic/expressions/coerce.tex` adds the `coerce[\T\]`
303	library identity function.
304	
305	**What it would buy.** One declaration inside `V`:
306	
307	```
308	  coerce(d: RR64) = V(d, emptyList[\V\](), emptyList[\RR64\]())
309	```
310	
311	would delete `konst` entirely (13 call sites), plus lines 59, 64, 68, 69 —
312	`opr +(self, c: RR64)`, `opr -(self, c: RR64)`, `opr /(self, c: RR64)`,
313	`opr /(self, n: ZZ32)` — and let `x - c`, `a + 0.00001`, `loss / 3.0` read
314	literally.
315	
316	**Probe.** `probes-spec/p3_coerce.fss` and `p3b_coerce_fn.fss` and `p15_coertc.fss`.
317	The declaration **parses** (no syntax error) but is ignored:
318	
319	```
320	$ fortress p15_coertc.fss
321	f got W
322	Unification error: Closure/Constructor for f param 1 (u:U) got arg 3: ZZ32 of type Int
323	
324	$ fortress typecheck p15_coertc.fss
325	    Could not check call to function f
326	    - U->String is not applicable to an argument of type IntLiteral.
327	File p15_coertc.fss has 1 error.
328	```
329

397	## 7. Why Σ is closed to `V` — spec-level *and* implementation-level, revised
398	
399	The journal's "P3, why `SUM` is closed" concluded impossibility. Both halves of
400	the answer are now precise, and the *reason* differs from what was recorded.
401	
402	**(i) Library sealing, not spec design.** `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3041`:
403	
404	```
405	opr SUM[\T extends Number\](): Comprehension[\T,Number,Number,Number\] = …
406	```
407	
408	The `T extends Number` constraint is the library's choice; the spec's
409	`opr BIG Op[\T\](g:…)` places no such constraint (§`reduction-expr`, above), and
410	`figref{generatedExpressions}` in `defining-generators.tex` shows `Σ` with a
411	generic `N`. `V` cannot become a `Number` because `trait Number … comprises {
412	RR64 }` (`FortressLibrary.fss:349`) is sealed — again a library decision.
413	
414	**(ii) But the spec *also* forbids the overload, for a different reason.**
415	`Specification/basic/overloading.tex`, §`overloading-terms`:
416	
417	> Although there may be multiple declarations with the same functional name, it
418	> is an error for their static parameters to differ (up to α-equivalence), or
419	> for one declaration to have static parameters and another to not have them.
420	
421	A user `opr SUM(…)` with no static parameters may not coexist with the library's
422	`opr SUM[\T extends Number\](…)`. This is a **spec-level** bar, independent of
423	the library.
424	
425	**(iii) And the implementation adds a third, narrower bar.** Probe
426	`probes-spec/p6_sum.fss`:
427	
428	```
429	Overloading of BIG +[\T extends Number\]():Comprehension[…]  …:3041  and
430	BIG +():Comprehension[\V,V,List[\V\],List[\V\]\]  …:22
431	fails because their parameter lists have the same types
432	```
433	
434	Both nullary registrations have parameter list `()`, so **at most one big
435	operator per name, per program** — which is what the file's header records
436	("nullary big-operator registrations are one-per-name") and what forced the
437	second glyph `BIG BOXPLUS`. Under the spec's single-declaration form (finding 6)
438	this collision would not exist, because the declarations would differ in their
439	real argument types.
440	
441	**Verdict for the charge:** the closedness of Σ is *both* a library sealing and a
442	spec-level restriction, and the one-per-name collision on top is purely an
443	implementation artefact of a desugaring the spec does not describe. The file's
444	choice of `BIG OPLUS`/`BIG BOXPLUS` is **(c) DELIBERATE and correct**; the header
445	comment's diagnosis ("the second-monoid worry turns out to be per-NAME, not
446	per-carrier") is right.

450	## 8. (b) SPEC-ONLY — multifix operators would give the n-ary `Sum` node for free
451	
452	This is the one the authors had no reason to look for, and it is aimed squarely
453	at the engine's central design decision.
454	
455	**Spec.** `Specification/basic/operators/chained-multifix.tex`, §`chained-multifix`:
456	
457	> Any infix operator that does not chain may be treated as *multifix*. If `n−1`
458	> occurrences of the same operator separate `n` operands where `n ≥ 3`, then the
459	> compiler **first checks to see whether there is a definition for that operator
460	> that will accept `n` arguments. If so, that definition is used**; if not, then
461	> the operator is treated as left-associative …
462	
463	The entire reason `microgpt_paper.fss` carries `vsum`, `VConcat` and
464	`opr BIG OPLUS` (lines 87–103, and the header's "alternative A: a uniform tape
465	node, summation as an n-ary Sum node built by BIG OPLUS over a list-concatenation
466	monoid") is to get **one** `Sum` node with `n` addends instead of a chain of
467	binary `+` nodes. A multifix declaration
468	
469	```
470	opr +(args: V...): V = V(SUM[a <- seq(args)] a.data, <| a | a <- seq(args) |>, …)
471	```
472	
473	is the spec's sanctioned way to get exactly that for ordinary infix `a + b + c`.
474	
475	**Probes.** `probes-spec/p12_multifix.fss`, `p13_multifix2.fss`.
476	Varargs declarations *are* supported. Multifix *dispatch* is not:
477	
478	- `opr OTIMES(a:V,b:V)` together with `opr OTIMES(args:V...)` is rejected —
479	  "*fails because of ambiguity in overlapping rest (...) parameters*".
480	- With only the varargs declaration, `a OTIMES b OTIMES c` yields
481	  `V(24.0, n=2)` — the value is right (2·3·4) but the node has **2** children:
482	  the expression was reassociated left-associatively into two binary calls. No
483	  `n`-argument definition was looked for.
484	
485	So the interpreter never performs the "first check for an `n`-argument
486	definition" step. **Revival-worklist item.** Our `BIG OPLUS`-over-a-concatenation-
487	monoid construction is **(c) DELIBERATE** and remains the only working route —
488	but it is a reconstruction of a language feature, which is exactly what this
489	audit was asked to find.

597	\section{Type Aliases}
598	\seclabel{type-alias}
599	
600	\begin{Grammar}
601	\emph{TypeAlias} &::=& \KWD{type} \emph{Id} \option{\emph{StaticParams}}
602	\EXP{=} \emph{Type} \\
603	\end{Grammar}
604	
605	Fortress allows names to serve as aliases for more complex type
606	instantiations.  A \emph{type alias} begins
607	with \KWD{type} followed by the name of the alias
608	type, followed by optional static parameters,
609	followed by \EXP{=}, followed by the type it stands for.
610	Parameterized type aliases are allowed but recursively
611	defined type aliases are not.  Here are some examples:
612	%type IntList = List[\ZZ64\]
613	%type BinOp = Float BY Float -> Float
614	%type SimpleFloat[\nat e, nat s\] = DetailedFloat[\Unity,e,s,false,false,false,false,true\]
615	\begin{Fortress}
616	\(\KWD{type} \TYP{IntList} = \TYP{List}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket\)\\
617	\(\KWD{type} \TYP{BinOp} = \TYP{Float} \times \TYP{Float} \rightarrow \TYP{Float}\)\\
618	\(\KWD{type} \TYP{SimpleFloat}\llbracket\KWD{nat} e, \KWD{nat} s\rrbracket = \TYP{DetailedFloat}\llbracket\TYP{Unity},e,s,\VAR{false},\VAR{false},\VAR{false},\VAR{false},\VAR{true}\rrbracket\)
619	\end{Fortress}
620	
621	All uses of type aliases are expanded before type checking.
622	Type aliases do not define new types nor
623	nominal equivalence relations among types.

12	\chapter{Types}
13	\chaplabel{types}
14	
15	\note{This chapter should be revised according to Victor's tuple story
16	(his email titled ``Tuple story'' on 12/07/07).}
17	
18	\note{Dimensions and units, type aliases, and some types in \secref{types-libraries}
19	are not yet supported.}
20	
21	The Fortress type system supports a mixture of nominal and structural types.
22	Specifically,
23	Fortress provides nominal trait types,
24	and dimension types (i.e., dimension types are also nominal)
25	which are defined in programs (often in libraries),
26	and a few constructs that combine types structurally.
27	\note{
28	Victor: This doesn't cover the special types, dimension types,
29	 or object expression types.  But I think it's okay for this intro,
30	 as long as we don't assert that these are all the types.
31	}
32	
33	Every expression has a \emph{static type},
34	and every value has a \emph{runtime type}
35	(also known as a \emph{dynamic type}).
36	Fortress programs are checked before they are executed to ensure that if
37	an expression $e$ evaluates to a value $v$, the runtime type of $v$ is a
38	subtype of the static type of $e$.
39	Sometimes we abuse terminology by saying that
40	an expression has the runtime type of the value it evaluates to
41	(see \secref{eval-completion} for a discussion about evaluation of expressions).

  private def buildCompilationUnitIndex(ast: CompilationUnit, modifiedDate: Long,
                                        errors: JavaList[StaticError],
                                        isApi: Boolean): CompilationUnitIndex = {
    val variables: JavaMap[Id, Variable] = new JavaHashMap[Id, Variable]()
    val initializers: JavaSet[VarDecl] = new JavaHashSet[VarDecl]()
    val functions: Relation[IdOrOpOrAnonymousName, JavaFunction] =
      new IndexedRelation[IdOrOpOrAnonymousName, JavaFunction](false)
    val parametricOperators: JavaSet[ParametricOperator] =
      new JavaHashSet[ParametricOperator]()
    val typeConses: JavaMap[Id, TypeConsIndex] = new JavaHashMap[Id, TypeConsIndex]()
    val dimensions: JavaMap[Id, JavaDimension] = new JavaHashMap[Id, JavaDimension]()
    val units: JavaMap[Id, JavaUnit] = new JavaHashMap[Id, JavaUnit]()
    val grammars: JavaMap[String, GrammarIndex] = new JavaHashMap[String, GrammarIndex]()
    val apiName = if (isApi) Some(ast.getName) else None

    // Make a mutable multimap to hold the coercions to each trait.
    val liftedCoercions = new HashMap[String, Set[Coercion]] with MultiMap[String, Coercion]

    for (decl <- ast.getDecls) {
      decl match {
        case d@STraitDecl(_, _, self, excludes, comprises, _) =>
          buildTrait(d, apiName, typeConses, functions, parametricOperators, errors)
          checkTraitClauses(typeConses, NU.getName(d),
                            NU.getStaticParams(d),
                            excludes, comprises, self)
        case d:ObjectDecl =>
          buildObject(d, apiName, typeConses, functions, parametricOperators, variables, errors)
        case d:VarDecl =>
          buildVariables(d, variables)
          if (! isApi) initializers.add(d)
        case d:FnDecl => buildFunction(d, apiName, functions, liftedCoercions)
        case d:DimDecl => buildDimension(d, dimensions)
        case d:UnitDecl => buildUnit(d, units)
        case d:GrammarDecl => if (isApi) buildGrammar(d, grammars, errors)
        case d:TypeAlias => bug("Not yet implemented: " + d)
        case d:TestDecl => bug("Not yet implemented: " + d)
        case d:PropertyDecl => bug("Not yet implemented: " + d)
        case _ =>
      }
    }

    // Add lifted coercions that were found.
    addLiftedCoercions(typeConses, liftedCoercions)
    if (isApi)
      new ApiIndex(ast.asInstanceOf[Api], variables, functions, parametricOperators,
                   typeConses, dimensions, units, grammars, modifiedDate)
    else
      new ComponentIndex(ast.asInstanceOf[Component], variables, initializers,
                         functions, parametricOperators,
                         typeConses, dimensions, units, modifiedDate)
  }

72	There are special type-like constructs called \emph{dimensions} that are
73	separate from other types (described in \chapref{types}).
74	There are also special constructs that modify types and values called
75	\emph{units} that are instances of dimensions.
76	These are used to describe physical quantities.
77	
78	\Library\ define dimensions and units for the standard SI system of measurement
79	based on meters, kilograms, seconds, amperes, and so on (as described in
80	\secref{lib:siunits}).   \Library\ also provide
81	supplemental units of measurement, such as feet and miles (as described in
82	\secref{lib:englishunits}).  For example,
83	\library\ provide a dimension named \TYP{Length} whose default unit is named
84	\TYP{meter} and abbreviated \verb$m_$.
85	By rendering convention, this abbreviation is rendered in roman type
86	without the underscore: \EXP{\mathrm{m}}. In contrast, the variable \txt{m} is rendered as in standard
87	mathematical notation: \VAR{m}.
88	See \secref{rendering} for a discussion of formatting conventions for tokens.
89	
90	For readability, plural forms of the unit names are defined as equivalent to the
91	corresponding singular forms; thus one can write \EXP{\TYP{meters} \mathbin{\TYP{per}} \TYP{second}},
92	for example.
93	Standard SI prefixes may be used on both the name and the symbol, so that \TYP{nanometer}
94	and \EXP{\mathrm{nm}} are also units of the dimension named \TYP{Length}, related to \TYP{meter}
95	and \EXP{\mathrm{m}} by a conversion factor of $10^{-9}$.
96	
97	Every dimension may have a default unit that is used for representing
98	values of quantities of that dimension if no unit is specified explicitly.
99	\Library\ define these default dimensions and units:
100	
101	\begin{tabular}{ll@{\hspace{2\tabcolsep}}ll}
102	\TYP{Length} & \TYP{meter} & \TYP{MagneticFlux} & \TYP{weber} \\
103	\TYP{Mass} & \TYP{kilogram} & \TYP{MagneticFluxDensity} & \TYP{tesla} \\
104	\TYP{Time} & \TYP{second} & \TYP{Inductance} & \TYP{henry} \\
105	\TYP{Frequency} & \TYP{hertz} & \TYP{Velocity} & \EXP{\TYP{meters} \mathbin{\TYP{per}} \TYP{second}} \\
106	\TYP{Force} & \TYP{newton} & \TYP{Acceleration} & \EXP{\TYP{meters} \mathbin{\TYP{per}} \TYP{second}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{squared}} \\
107	\TYP{Pressure} & \TYP{pascal} & \TYP{Angle} & \TYP{radian} \\
108	\TYP{Energy} & \TYP{joule} & \TYP{SolidAngle} & \TYP{steradian} \\
109	\TYP{Power} & \TYP{watt} & \TYP{LuminousIntensity} & \TYP{candela} \\
110	\TYP{Temperature} & \TYP{kelvin} & \TYP{LuminousFlux} & \TYP{lumen} \\
111	\TYP{Area} & \EXP{\mathbin{\TYP{square}}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{meter}} & \TYP{Illuminance} & \TYP{lux} \\
112	\TYP{Volume} & \EXP{\mathbin{\TYP{cubic}}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{meter}} & \TYP{RadionuclideActivity} & \TYP{becquerel} \\
113	\TYP{ElectricCurrent} & \TYP{ampere} & \TYP{AbsorbedDose} & \TYP{gray} \\
114	\TYP{ElectricCharge} & \TYP{coulomb} & \TYP{DoseEquivalent} & \VAR{sievert} \\
115	\TYP{ElectricPotential} & \TYP{volt} & \TYP{AmountOfSubstance} & \TYP{mole} \\
116	\TYP{Capacitance} & \TYP{farad} & \TYP{CatalyticActivity} & \TYP{katal} \\
117	\TYP{Resistance} & \TYP{ohm} & \TYP{MassDensity} & \EXP{\TYP{kilograms} \mathbin{\TYP{per}} \mathbin{\TYP{cubic}}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{meter}} \\
118	\TYP{Conductance} & \TYP{siemens} \\
119	\end{tabular}
120	
121	
122	In addition, \library\ define the dimension \TYP{Information} with
123	units \TYP{bit} and \TYP{byte}
124	(and the plurals \TYP{bits} and \TYP{bytes}), a \TYP{byte} being equal to 8
125	\TYP{bits}.
126	To avoid confusion, SI prefixes are \emph{not} provided for these units;
127	instead, programmers must
128	use appropriate powers of 2 or 10, for example \EXP{10^{6}
129	  \TYP{bits}} or \EXP{2^{20} \TYP{bits}}.
130	
131	Here are some examples of the use of dimensions and units:
132	%x: RR64 Length = 1.3 m_
133	%t: RR64 Time = 5 s_
134	%v: RR64 Velocity = x / t
135	%w: RR64 Velocity in nm_/s_ = 17 nm_/s_
136	%x: RR64 Velocity in furlongs per fortnight = v in furlongs per fortnight
137	\begin{Fortress}
138	\(x\COLON \mathbb{R}64\,\TYP{Length} = 1.3\,\mathrm{m}\)\\
139	\(t\COLON \mathbb{R}64\,\TYP{Time} = 5\,\mathrm{s}\)\\
140	\(v\COLON \mathbb{R}64\,\TYP{Velocity} = x / t\)\\
141	\(w\COLON \mathbb{R}64\,\TYP{Velocity}\, \KWD{in}\, \mathrm{nm}/\mathrm{s} = 17\,\mathrm{nm}/\mathrm{s}\)\\
142	\(x\COLON \mathbb{R}64\,\TYP{Velocity}\, \KWD{in}\, \TYP{furlongs} \mathbin{\TYP{per}} \TYP{fortnight} = v\, \KWD{in}\, \TYP{furlongs} \mathbin{\TYP{per}} \TYP{fortnight}\)
143	\end{Fortress}
144	
145	
146	
147	Dimensions and units can be multiplied, divided, and raised to rational powers to produce new dimensions and units. Both the numerator and the denominator of a rational power of a dimension or a unit must be a valid \emph{\KWD{nat} parameter} instantiation
148	(as described in \secref{natparams}).
149	Multiplication can be expressed using juxtaposition or \EXP{\cdot};
150	division can be expressed using \EXP{/} or \TYP{per}.
151	The syntactic operators \TYP{square} and \TYP{cubic} may be applied to a dimension or unit in order to raise
152	it to the second power, third power, respectively; the special postfix syntactic operators \TYP{squared}
153	and \TYP{cubed} may be used for the same purpose.
154	The syntactic operator \TYP{inverse} may be applied to a dimension or unit to divide it into 1.
155	All of these syntactic operators are merely syntactic sugar, expanded before type checking.
156	
157	\note{I manually added a space between inverse and ohms below.}
158	%grams per cubic centimeter
159	%meter per second squared
160	%inverse ohms
161	\begin{Fortress}
162	\(\TYP{grams} \mathbin{\TYP{per}} \mathbin{\TYP{cubic}}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{centimeter} \)\\
163	\(\TYP{meter} \mathbin{\TYP{per}} \TYP{second}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{squared} \)\\
164	\(\mathbin{\TYP{inverse}}\ \TYP{ohms}\)
165	\end{Fortress}
166	
167	One can also write \EXP{1/X} as a synonym for \EXP{X^{-1}} if
168	\VAR{X} is either a dimension or a unit.
169	
170	Most numerical values in Fortress are dimensionless quantity values.
171	Multiplying or dividing a dimensionless value by a unit produces a dimensioned value;
172	thus \EXP{5\,\mathrm{s}} is the dimensioned value equal to five seconds, which has
173	numerical value \EXP{5} and \TYP{second} for its unit.
174	A dimensioned value may also be
175	multiplied or divided by a unit, and the result is to combine the units;
176	the expression
177	%% \EXP{17\,\mathrm{nm}/\mathrm{s}}
178	\EXP{(17\,\mathrm{nm})/\mathrm{s}}
179	first multiplies \EXP{17} by
180	\EXP{\mathrm{nm}} to produce the dimensioned value seventeen nanometers,
181	which is then divided by the unit \EXP{\mathrm{s}}
182	to produce seventeen nanometers per second.
183	
184	The unit of a dimensioned value may be changed to another unit of the same dimension
185	by using the \KWD{in} operator, which takes a quantity to its left and a unit to its right.
186	The \KWD{in} operator changes the unit and multiplies or divides the numerical value
187	by an appropriate conversion constant so as to preserve the overall dimensioned value.
188	Thus \EXP{1.3\,\mathrm{m}\, \KWD{in}\, \mathrm{nm}} produces \EXP{1 300 000 000\,\mathrm{nm}}.
189	
190	Multiplying or dividing a dimensionless numerical type by a unit produces an equivalent
191	dimensioned numerical type with that unit associated; thus \EXP{\mathbb{R}64\,\TYP{meter}} is a
192	type that is just like \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} but whose values are values of dimension
193	\TYP{Length} measured in \TYP{meters}.  A dimensioned numerical type may be
194	further multiplied or divided by a unit.
195	As a convenience,
196	if a dimension has a default unit, a numerical type may
197	also be multiplied or divided by a dimension, in which case the result is as if
198	the default unit for that dimension had been used.
199	The \KWD{in} operator may also
200	be used to change the unit associated with a dimensioned type; in this situation
201	the effect is merely to alter the unit associated with the type; no numerical
202	operation is performed at run time.
203	
204	Certain aggregate types, such as \TYP{Vector}, may also have associated units.
205	
206	There are two reasons for using dimensions and units.  One is that the \KWD{in}
207	operator can supply conversion factors automatically.  The other is that
208	certain programming errors may be detected at compile time.
209	When dimensioned values are added, subtracted, or compared,
210	it is a static error if the units do not match.
211	When dimensioned values are multiplied or divided, their units
212	are multiplied or divided.  When taking the square root of a dimensioned
213	value, the unit of the result is the square root of the argument's unit.
214	Other numerical functions, such as \EXP{\sin} and \EXP{\log}, require
215	dimensionless arguments.
216	
217	A variable whose declared
218	type includes a dimension without an accompanying unit
219	is understood to have the default unit for that dimension.
220	Thus, in most cases, the runtime unit of an expression can be statically
221	inferred. However, there are exceptions. For example,
222	consider the following declaration:
223	\note{I manually edited the array type.}
224	% a : Object[3] = [5 mg_, 3 m_, 4 s_]
225	\begin{Fortress}
226	{\tt~}\pushtabs\=\+\( a \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \TYP{Object}[3] = [5\,\mathrm{mg}, 3\,\mathrm{m}, 4\,\mathrm{s}]\)\-\\\poptabs
227	\end{Fortress}
228	
229	Now suppose we declare a function that takes an array of objects and returns
230	one of its elements:
231	\note{I manually edited the array type.}
232	% f(xs:Object[3]) = xs[1]
233	\begin{Fortress}
234	{\tt~}\pushtabs\=\+\( f(\VAR{xs}\COLONOP\TYP{Object}[3]) = \VAR{xs}_{1}\)\-\\\poptabs
235	\end{Fortress}
236	
237	The value of the call \EXP{f(a)} is \EXP{3\,\mathrm{m}}. However, the static
238	type of  \EXP{f(a)} is simply \TYP{Object}. When the value \EXP{3\,\mathrm{m}}
239	is placed in an array of objects, the value is boxed, and the unit associated
240	with the value must be included as part of the boxed value. However, unboxed
241	values need not include unit information at runtime, as this information is
242	statically evident in such cases.
243	
244	\note{Guy's explanation ---
245	The thing to understand is that a measurement is a value object,
246	but storing it in an \EXP{\TYP{Array}\llbracket\TYP{Object}\rrbracket} will force the value object
247	to be boxed.  Boxing causes type information to be associated
248	with the value.  Unit information is not really ``erased'' at compile
249	time; rather, unit information is ``static'', that is, part of the type,
250	and so the unit information can be omitted from a run-time
251	representation exactly when type information can be omitted from
252	a run-time representation.  The situation is exactly the same as for
253	dimensionless numerical types such as ints and floats.}
254	
255	
256	There are also special static parameters for units and dimensions; see
257	\secref{dimunitparams}.

12	\chapter{Dimension and Unit Declarations}
13	\chaplabel{declaring-dimunits}
14	
15	\note{Dimensions and units are not yet supported.}
16	
17	\begin{Grammar}
18	\emph{DimUnitDecl}
19	&::=&
20	\KWD{dim} \emph{Id} \options{\EXP{=} \emph{Type}}
21	(\KWD{unit} $|$ \KWD{SI\_unit}) \emph{Id}$^+$
22	\options{\EXP{=} \emph{Expr}}\\
23	&$|$&
24	\KWD{dim} \emph{Id}
25	\options{\EXP{=} \emph{Type}} \options{\KWD{default} \emph{Id}}\\
26	&$|$&
27	(\KWD{unit} $|$ \KWD{SI\_unit})
28	\emph{Id}$^+$ \options{\EXP{\mathrel{\mathtt{:}}} \emph{Type}}
29	 \options{\EXP{=} \emph{Expr}}\\
30	\end{Grammar}
31	
32	\section{Dimension Declarations}
33	Dimensions may be explicitly declared;
34	every declared dimension must be declared at the top level
35	of a program component,
36	not within a block expression or trait.
37	Other dimensions may be constructed by multiplying and dividing other dimensions,
38	as described in \chapref{dimunits}.
39	An explicitly declared dimension may be a \emph{base dimension} (with no definition specified)
40	or a \emph{derived dimension} (with a definition specified in the form of an initialization expression).
41	
42	The set of all dimensions has the algebraic structure of a free abelian group.
43	The identity element of this group is the dimension \TYP{Unity}, which represents dimensionlessness.
44	
45	For every two dimensions \VAR{D} and \VAR{E}, there is a
46	dimension \EXP{D E} (which may also be written \EXP{D \cdot E}),
47	corresponding to the product of the dimensions \VAR{D} and \VAR{E} and a
48	dimension \EXP{D/E}, corresponding to the quotient of the
49	dimensions \VAR{D} and \VAR{E}. The syntactic sugar \EXP{1/D} is equivalent
50	to \EXP{\TYP{Unity}/D} for all dimensions \VAR{D}.
51	A dimension can be raised to a rational power where both
52	the numerator and the denominator of the rational power
53	must be a valid \emph{\KWD{nat} parameter} instantiation;
54	\EXP{D^{0}} is the same as \TYP{Unity},
55	\EXP{D^{1}} is the same as \VAR{D}, and
56	\EXP{D^{m+n}} is the same as \EXP{D^{m} D^{n}}.
57	The syntactic sugar \EXP{D^{-n}} is the same as \EXP{\TYP{Unity}/D^{n}}.
58	
59	Here are some examples of base dimension declarations:
60	%% dim Length
61	%% dim Mass
62	%% dim Time
63	%% dim ElectricCurrent
64	\begin{Fortress}
65	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Length}\)\\
66	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Mass}\)\\
67	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Time}\)\\
68	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{ElectricCurrent}\)
69	\end{Fortress}
70	Here are some examples of computed dimensions:
71	%% Length / Time
72	%% Velocity / Time
73	%% Length \cdot Mass / Time^2
74	%% Length Mass Time^(-2)
75	%% ElectricCurrent / Length^2
76	\begin{Fortress}
77	\(\TYP{Length} / \TYP{Time}\)\\
78	\(\TYP{Velocity} / \TYP{Time}\)\\
79	\(\TYP{Length} \cdot \TYP{Mass} / \TYP{Time}^{2}\)\\
80	\(\TYP{Length}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Mass}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Time}^{-2}\)\\
81	\(\TYP{ElectricCurrent} / \TYP{Length}^{2}\)
82	\end{Fortress}
83	and here some of these computed dimensions are given names through the use of
84	derived dimension declarations:
85	%% dim Velocity = Length / Time
86	%% dim Acceleration = Velocity / Time
87	%% dim CurrentDensity = ElectricCurrent / Length^2
88	\begin{Fortress}
89	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Velocity} = \TYP{Length} / \TYP{Time}\)\\
90	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Acceleration} = \TYP{Velocity} / \TYP{Time}\)\\
91	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{CurrentDensity} = \TYP{ElectricCurrent} / \TYP{Length}^{2}\)
92	\end{Fortress}
93	
94	\section{Unit Declarations}
95	Every unit belongs to exactly one dimension, which is the type of the unit.
96	A dimension may have more than one unit,
97	but one of these units may be singled out as the \emph{default unit} for that dimension
98	by adding a \KWD{default} clause:
99	%% dim Length default meter
100	%% dim Mass default kilogram
101	%% dim Time default second
102	\begin{Fortress}
103	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Length} \KWD{default} \TYP{meter}\)\\
104	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Mass} \KWD{default} \TYP{kilogram}\)\\
105	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Time} \KWD{default} \TYP{second}\)
106	\end{Fortress}
107	The default unit is used when a numerical type is multiplied by a
108	dimension to produce a new type (see \chapref{dimunits}).
109	If no default clause is specified for a base dimension, then it has
110	no default unit.  If no default clause is specified for a derived
111	dimension, then it has a default unit if and only if all the
112	dimensions mentioned in its initialization expression have defaults,
113	in which case its default unit is calculated using the initialization
114	expression with each dimension replaced by its default unit.
115	
116	Some units are explicitly declared;
117	every declared unit must be declared at the top level of
118	a program component, not
119	within a block expression or trait.
120	Other units may be constructed by multiplying and dividing other units.
121	An explicitly declared unit may be a \emph{base unit} (with no definition specified)
122	or a \emph{derived unit} (with a definition specified in the form of an initialization expression).
123	
124	The set of all units, like the set of all dimensions, has the algebraic structure of a free abelian group.
125	The identity element of this group is the unit \TYP{dimensionless}, of
126	dimension \TYP{Unity}.
127	Note that there may be other units of dimension \TYP{Unity}, such as
128	\TYP{radian} and \TYP{steradian}, but only \TYP{dimensionless} is the
129	identity of the group of all units.
130	(Note that there is a straightforward homomorphism of units onto
131	dimensions, wherein every unit is mapped to its dimension.)
132	
133	Here are some examples of base unit declarations:
134	%% unit meter : Length
135	%% unit kilogram : Mass
136	%% unit second : Time
137	%% unit ampere : ElectricCurrent
138	\begin{Fortress}
139	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{meter} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \TYP{Length}\)\\
140	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{kilogram} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \TYP{Mass}\)\\
141	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{second} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \TYP{Time}\)\\
142	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{ampere} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \TYP{ElectricCurrent}\)
143	\end{Fortress}
144	Here are some examples of computed units:
145	%% meter / second
146	%% (meter / second) / second
147	%% meter \cdot kilogram / second^2
148	%% meter kilogram second^(-2)
149	%% ampere / meter^2
150	\begin{Fortress}
151	\(\TYP{meter} / \TYP{second}\)\\
152	\((\TYP{meter} / \TYP{second}) / \TYP{second}\)\\
153	\(\TYP{meter} \cdot \TYP{kilogram} / \TYP{second}^{2}\)\\
154	\(\TYP{meter}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{kilogram}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{second}^{-2}\)\\
155	\(\TYP{ampere} / \TYP{meter}^{2}\)
156	\end{Fortress}
157	and here some computed units are given names through the use of
158	derived unit declarations:
159	%% unit newton: Force = meter \cdot kilogram / second^2
160	%% unit joule: Energy = newton meter
161	%% unit pascal: Pressure = newton / meter^2
162	\begin{Fortress}
163	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{newton}\COLON \TYP{Force} = \TYP{meter} \cdot \TYP{kilogram} / \TYP{second}^{2}\)\\
164	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{joule}\COLON \TYP{Energy} = \TYP{newton}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{meter}\)\\
165	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{pascal}\COLON \TYP{Pressure} = \TYP{newton} / \TYP{meter}^{2}\)
166	\end{Fortress}
167	In the preceding examples, the initialization expression for each unit
168	is itself a unit.  It is also permitted for the initialization
169	expression to be a dimensioned numerical value, in which case
170	the unit being declared is related to the unit of the dimensioned
171	numerical value by a numerical conversion factor.
172	
173	As with an ordinary variable declaration, one may omit the dimension for a unit
174	if there is an initialization expression; the dimension of the declared unit is
175	the dimension of the unit of the expression.
176	
177	\note{COMMENTED TEXT; I like the explanation below better. -- Eric
178	
179	Every unit can be reduced to a canonical unit as follows.  A base unit is
180	canonical; a \KWD{unit} parameter is canonical; a defined unit is replaced
181	by its initialization expression,
182	but only if the value of the expression
183	is a unit and not a dimensioned value, where every unit in that expression
184	is replaced by its canonical unit;
185	and finally all arithmetic is performed
186	so as to reduce the expression to a single unit. Two units are considered
187	equivalent if their canonical units are identical.
188	
189	Now here is a slightly different process.
190	}
191	
192	Every unit can be reduced to a canonical value as follows.  A base unit is
193	multiplied by the value \EXP{1}; a \KWD{unit} parameter is multiplied by
194	the value \EXP{1}; a defined unit is replaced by its initialization
195	expression and then every unit in that expression is replaced by its
196	canonical form;
197	and finally all arithmetic is performed so as to reduce the
198	units to a single unit and the
199	numerical values to a single numerical value.  A dimensioned value with unit
200	\VAR{U} is convertible by the \KWD{in} operator to a value with unit
201	\VAR{V} if the canonical values for \VAR{U} and \VAR{V} have the same
202	unit; the conversion involves multiplying the numerical value by the
203	ratio of the numerical value of the canonical form
204	of \VAR{V} to the numerical value of the canonical form of \VAR{U}.
205	
206	For example, given the declarations:
207	%% dim Length
208	%% unit meter: Length; unit meters = meter
209	%% unit kilometer: Length = 10^3 meter; unit kilometers = kilometer
210	%% unit inch: Length = 2.54 \times 10^(-2) meter; unit inches = inch
211	%% unit foot: Length = 12 inch; unit feet = foot
212	%% unit mile: Length = 5280 foot; unit miles = mile
213	\begin{Fortress}
214	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Length}\)\\
215	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{meter}\COLON \TYP{Length}; \KWD{unit} \TYP{meters} = \TYP{meter}\)\\
216	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{kilometer}\COLON \TYP{Length} = 10^{3} \TYP{meter}; \KWD{unit} \TYP{kilometers} = \TYP{kilometer}\)\\
217	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{inch}\COLON \TYP{Length} = 2.54 \times 10^{-2} \TYP{meter}; \KWD{unit} \TYP{inches} = \TYP{inch} \)\\
218	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{foot}\COLON \TYP{Length} = 12\,\TYP{inch}; \KWD{unit} \TYP{feet} = \TYP{foot}\)\\
219	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{mile}\COLON \TYP{Length} = 5280\,\TYP{foot}; \KWD{unit} \TYP{miles} = \TYP{mile}\)
220	\end{Fortress}
221	then one can say \EXP{3\,\TYP{miles}\, \KWD{in}\, \TYP{kilometers}} and
222	the \KWD{in} operator will multiply the numerical value \EXP{3} by
223	the amount of
224	\EXP{((2.54 \times 10^{-2})(12)(5280)/10^{3})},
225	or \EXP{25146/15625}.
226	
227	Notice the subtle difference between these two declarations:
228	%% unit radian = meter/meter
229	%% unit radian = 1 meter/meter
230	\begin{Fortress}
231	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{radian} = \TYP{meter}/\TYP{meter}\)\\
232	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{radian} = 1\,\TYP{meter}/\TYP{meter}\)
233	\end{Fortress}
234	The first declaration defines \TYP{radian} to be equivalent to
235	\TYP{dimensionless}, and so a value with unit \TYP{radian} can be used
236	anywhere a dimensionless value can be used, and vice versa.
237	The second declaration defines \TYP{radian} to be convertible to
238	\TYP{dimensionless} but not equivalent, and so it is necessary to use
239	the \KWD{in} operator (or multiplication and division by \TYP{radian})
240	to convert between values in radians and truly dimensionless values.
241	
242	
243	\section{Abbreviating Dimension and Unit Declarations}
244	\seclabel{abbrev-dimunits}
245	
246	For convenience, three forms of syntactic sugar are provided when declaring
247	dimensions and units.
248	First, in a \KWD{unit} declaration one may mention more than one name
249	before the colon, and the extra names are defined to be synonyms for the
250	first name; thus
251	%% unit foot feet ft_: Length
252	\begin{Fortress}
253	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{foot}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{feet}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{ft}\COLON \TYP{Length}\)
254	\end{Fortress}
255	means exactly the same thing as
256	%% unit foot: Length
257	%% unit feet: Length = foot
258	%% unit ft_: Length = foot
259	\begin{Fortress}
260	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{foot}\COLON \TYP{Length}\)\\
261	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{feet}\COLON \TYP{Length} = \TYP{foot}\)\\
262	\(\KWD{unit} \mathrm{ft}\COLON \TYP{Length} = \TYP{foot}\)
263	\end{Fortress}
264	Second, instead of the reserved word \KWD{unit} one may use the reserved
265	word \KWD{SI\_unit}, which has the effect of defining not only the
266	specified names but also names with the various SI prefixes attached.
267	If more than one name is specified, then the last name is assumed
268	to be a symbol and has symbol prefixes (such as \TYP{M} and \TYP{n})
269	attached; all other names have the full prefixes (such as
270	\TYP{mega} and \TYP{nano}) attached.
271	Thus
272	%% SI_unit name1 name2 name3: ...
273	\begin{Fortress}
274	\(\KWD{SI{\char'137}unit} {name}_{1}\;\;{name}_{2}\;\;{name}_{3}\COLON \ldots\)
275	\end{Fortress}
276	may be regarded as an abbreviation for
277	%% unit~name1~name2~name3: ...

292	%% unit nano~name1~nano name2~n name3 = 10^(-9) ~name1

296	%% unit zepto~name1~zepto name2~z name3 = 10^(-21) ~name1

300	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{yotta} {name}_{1}~\TYP{yotta} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{Y} {name}_{3} = 10^{24} {name}_{1}\)\\
301	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{zetta} {name}_{1}~\TYP{zetta} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{Z} {name}_{3} = 10^{21}  {name}_{1}\)\\

305	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{giga} {name}_{1}~\TYP{giga} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{G} {name}_{3} = 10^{9}  {name}_{1}\)\\
306	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{mega} {name}_{1}~\TYP{mega} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{M} {name}_{3} = 10^{6}  {name}_{1}\)\\
307	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{kilo} {name}_{1}~\TYP{kilo} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{k} {name}_{3} = 10^{3}  {name}_{1}\)\\
308	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{hecto} {name}_{1}~\TYP{hecto} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{h} {name}_{3} = 10^{2}  {name}_{1}\)\\
309	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{deka} {name}_{1}~\TYP{deka} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{da} {name}_{3} = 10  {name}_{1}\)\\
310	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{deci} {name}_{1}~\TYP{deci} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{d} {name}_{3} = 10^{-1}  {name}_{1}\)\\
311	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{centi} {name}_{1}~\TYP{centi} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{c} {name}_{3} = 10^{-2}  {name}_{1}\)\\
312	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{milli} {name}_{1}~\TYP{milli} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{m} {name}_{3} = 10^{-3}  {name}_{1}\)\\
313	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{micro} {name}_{1}~\TYP{micro} {name}_{2}~ \mu {name}_{3} = 10^{-6}  {name}_{1}\)\\
314	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{nano} {name}_{1}~\TYP{nano} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{n} {name}_{3} = 10^{-9}  {name}_{1}\)\\
315	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{pico} {name}_{1}~\TYP{pico} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{p} {name}_{3} = 10^{-12}  {name}_{1}\)\\
316	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{femto} {name}_{1}~\TYP{femto} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{f} {name}_{3} = 10^{-15}  {name}_{1}\)\\
317	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{atto} {name}_{1}~\TYP{atto} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{a} {name}_{3} = 10^{-18}  {name}_{1}\)\\
318	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{zepto} {name}_{1}~\TYP{zepto} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{z} {name}_{3} = 10^{-21}  {name}_{1}\)\\
319	\(\KWD{unit} \TYP{yocto} {name}_{1}~\TYP{yocto} {name}_{2}~ \TYP{y} {name}_{3} = 10^{-24}  {name}_{1}\)
320	\end{Fortress}
321	where $\mu$ is the Unicode character U+00B5 MICRO SIGN.
322	Third, a \KWD{dim} declaration and a \KWD{unit} or
323	\EXP{\KWD{SI{\char'137}unit}} declaration
324	may be collapsed into a single declaration by writing the \KWD{unit}
325	or \EXP{\KWD{SI{\char'137}unit}}
326	declaration in place of the \KWD{default} clause in the \KWD{dim} declaration
327	and omitting the colon and dimension from the \KWD{unit} declaration.
328	Thus
329	%% dim Length  SI_unit meter meters m_
330	%% dim Power = Energy/Time  SI_unit watt watts W_ = joule/second
331	\begin{Fortress}
332	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Length}  \KWD{SI{\char'137}unit} \TYP{meter}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{meters}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}\)\\
333	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Power} = \TYP{Energy}/\TYP{Time}  \KWD{SI{\char'137}unit} \TYP{watt}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{watts}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{W} = \TYP{joule}/\TYP{second}\)
334	\end{Fortress}
335	is understood to abbreviate
336	%% dim Length default meter; SI_unit meter meters m_: Length
337	%% dim Power = Energy/Time default watt; SI_unit watt watts W_: Power = joule/second
338	\begin{Fortress}
339	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Length} \KWD{default} \TYP{meter}; \KWD{SI{\char'137}unit} \TYP{meter}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{meters}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m}\COLON \TYP{Length}\)\\
340	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Power} = \TYP{Energy}/\TYP{Time} \KWD{default} \TYP{watt}; \KWD{SI{\char'137}unit} \TYP{watt}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{watts}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{W}\COLON \TYP{Power} = \TYP{joule}/\TYP{second}\)
341	\end{Fortress}
342	In this way the names of the seven SI base units, along with all
343	possible plural and prefixed forms, may be concisely defined as follows:
344	%% dim Length  SI_unit meter meters m_
345	%% dim Mass default kilogram; SI_unit gram grams g_: Mass
346	%% dim Time  SI_unit second seconds s_
347	%% dim ElectricCurrent  SI_unit ampere amperes A_
348	%% dim Temperature  SI_unit kelvin kelvins K_
349	%% dim AmountOfSubstance  SI_unit mole moles mol_
350	%% dim LuminousIntensity  SI_unit candela candelas cd_
351	\begin{Fortress}
352	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Length}  \KWD{SI{\char'137}unit} \TYP{meter}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{meters}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{m} \)\\
353	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Mass} \KWD{default} \TYP{kilogram}; \KWD{SI{\char'137}unit} \TYP{gram}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{grams}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{g}\COLON \TYP{Mass}\)\\
354	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Time}  \KWD{SI{\char'137}unit} \TYP{second}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{seconds}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{s}\)\\
355	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{ElectricCurrent}  \KWD{SI{\char'137}unit} \TYP{ampere}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{amperes}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{A}\)\\
356	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{Temperature}  \KWD{SI{\char'137}unit} \TYP{kelvin}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{kelvins}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{K}\)\\
357	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{AmountOfSubstance}  \KWD{SI{\char'137}unit} \TYP{mole}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{moles}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{mol}\)\\
358	\(\KWD{dim} \TYP{LuminousIntensity}  \KWD{SI{\char'137}unit} \TYP{candela}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{candelas}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathrm{cd}\)
359	\end{Fortress}
360	Note the subtle difference in the declaration of \TYP{Mass} that
361	allows the default unit to be \TYP{kilogram} rather than \TYP{gram}.
362	
363	
364	\section{Absorbing Units}
365	\seclabel{absorbing-units}
366	
367	\begin{Grammar}
368	\emph{StaticParam}
369	&::=& \emph{Id} \option{\emph{Extends}} \options{\KWD{absorbs} \KWD{unit}} \\
370	&$|$& \KWD{unit} \emph{Id} \options{\EXP{\mathrel{\mathtt{:}}} \emph{Type}}
371	 \options{\KWD{absorbs} \KWD{unit}}\\
372	\end{Grammar}
373	
374	The declaration of a type parameter or a \KWD{unit} parameter for
375	a parameterized trait may contain a clause
376	``\EXP{\KWD{absorbs}\;\;\KWD{unit}}''; at
377	most one static parameter of a trait may have this clause.  An
378	instance of a parameterized trait
379	with a static parameter that ``\EXP{\KWD{absorbs}\;\;\KWD{unit}}'' may
380	be multiplied
381	or divided by a unit, the result being another instance of that
382	parameterized trait in which the static argument corresponding to
383	the unit-absorbing parameter has been multiplied or divided by the unit.
384	
385	A few examples should make this clear.  Given the declaration
386	%% trait Vector[\EltType extends Number absorbs unit, nat len\] \ldots end
387	\begin{Fortress}
388	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Vector}\llbracket\TYP{EltType} \KWD{extends} \TYP{Number} \KWD{absorbs}\;\;\KWD{unit}, \KWD{nat} \VAR{len}\rrbracket \ldots \KWD{end}\)
389	\end{Fortress}
390	then \EXP{\TYP{Vector}\llbracket\TYP{Float}, 3\rrbracket \TYP{meter}}
391	means the same as
392	\EXP{\TYP{Vector}\llbracket\TYP{Float}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{meter}, 3\rrbracket},
393	and \EXP{\TYP{Vector}\llbracket\TYP{Float}, 3\rrbracket /
394	  \TYP{second}} means the same as
395	\EXP{\TYP{Vector}\llbracket\TYP{Float} / \TYP{second}, 3\rrbracket}.
396	Therefore,
397	%[(3 m_) (2 m_) (5 m_)]
398	\EXP{[(3\,\mathrm{m}) (2\,\mathrm{m}) (5\,\mathrm{m})]}
399	means the same as
400	%[3 2 5] m_
401	\EXP{[3\;2\;5] \mathrm{m}}.
402	%
403	Similarly, given the declaration
404	%% trait Float[\unit U absorbs unit, nat e, nat s\] \ldots end
405	\begin{Fortress}
406	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Float}\llbracket\KWD{unit} U \KWD{absorbs}\;\;\KWD{unit}, \KWD{nat} e, \KWD{nat} s\rrbracket \ldots \KWD{end}\)
407	\end{Fortress}
408	then \EXP{\TYP{Float}\llbracket\TYP{meter}, 11, 53\rrbracket /
409	  \TYP{second}} means the same as
410	\EXP{\TYP{Float}\llbracket\TYP{meter} / \TYP{second}, 11, 53\rrbracket}, and
411	\begin{Fortress}
412	%% Float[\dimensionless, 8, 24\] meter kilogram / second^2
413	\EXP{\TYP{Float}\llbracket\mathbin{\TYP{dimensionless}}, 8, 24\rrbracket \TYP{meter}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{kilogram} / \TYP{second}^{2}}
414	\end{Fortress}
415	means the same as
416	\begin{Fortress}
417	%% Float[\dimensionless meter kilogram / second^2, 8, 24\]
418	\EXP{\TYP{Float}\llbracket\mathbin{\TYP{dimensionless}}\, \TYP{meter}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{kilogram} / \TYP{second}^{2}, 8, 24\rrbracket},
419	\end{Fortress}
420	which is the same as
421	%% Float[\meter kilogram / second^2, 8, 24\]
422	\begin{Fortress}
423	\EXP{\TYP{Float}\llbracket\TYP{meter}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{kilogram} / \TYP{second}^{2}, 8, 24\rrbracket}.
424	\end{Fortress}
425	This is the mechanism by which meaning is given to the multiplication
426	and division of library-defined types by units.
427

(* Q1 substitute B: the carrier object -- a six-line wrapper that IS a new
   nominal type but reads like a named space in signatures, and (per
   explorations/expressiveness-review.md finding 4, probe p14_genwrap.fss)
   buys |x|, x[i], generator integration.

   lifted into it.  Probing what it costs and what it buys. *)
component p9_carrier_subst
import List.{...}
export Executable

trait Rank1V excludes Rank2V end
trait Rank2V excludes Rank1V end

(* named space: a vector of reals *)
object Vec(xs: List[\RR64\]) extends { Rank1V, ZeroIndexed[\RR64\], DelegatedIndexed[\RR64,ZZ32\] }
  getter asString(): String = "" xs
  getter indices(): Generator[\ZZ32\] = 0#|xs|
  opr |self| : ZZ32 = |xs|
  opr [i: ZZ32]: RR64 = xs[i]
  opr [r: Range[\ZZ32\]]: ZeroIndexed[\RR64\] = Vec(xs[r])
end

(* named space: a probability distribution -- same representation, different name *)
object ProbDist(xs: List[\RR64\]) extends { Rank1V, ZeroIndexed[\RR64\], DelegatedIndexed[\RR64,ZZ32\] }
  getter asString(): String = "" xs
  getter indices(): Generator[\ZZ32\] = 0#|xs|
  opr |self| : ZZ32 = |xs|
  opr [i: ZZ32]: RR64 = xs[i]
  opr [r: Range[\ZZ32\]]: ZeroIndexed[\RR64\] = ProbDist(xs[r])
end

(* the signature now echoes the paper: softmax : R^n -> Delta^{n-1} *)
softmax(z: Vec): ProbDist = do
  e = <|[\RR64\] EXP(z[i]) | i <- 0#|z| |>
  s = SUM [ u <- e ] u
  ProbDist(<|[\RR64\] u / s | u <- e |>)
end

run() = do
  p = softmax(Vec(<|[\RR64\] 1.0, 2.0, 3.0|>))
  println("softmax = " p)
  println("sums to " (SUM [ i <- 0#|p| ] p[i]))
end

end
